attemper.md.primary: To reduce, modify, or moderate the strength or temperature of something by blending or dilution.
attemper.md.secondary: In historical metallurgy and brewing, to regulate heat or alcoholic potency by mixing countervailing elements.

quotes.author: Alexander Pope
quotes.quote: With skillful hand the gentle bards **attemper** their strains to soothe the grief of mourning heroes.

quotes.author: Richard Chenevix Trench
quotes.quote: If sweet with bitter were not wisely **attempered** still in human life, our character would remain untested.

quotes.author: Edmund Spenser
quotes.quote: She learned to **attemper** her flaming passions with wise discretion and mild counsel.

attempt.md.primary: To make an effort to achieve, perform, or accomplish something difficult or perilous.
attempt.md.secondary: In criminal jurisprudence, an overt act performed with specific intent to commit a crime beyond mere preparation.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: I'll stay at home, and pray God's blessing into thy **attempt**.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Oak cast his eyes down the field in a way implying that it was useless to **attempt** argument.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: Yet they seldom **attempt** to make out a list of the a priori principles which are to serve as the premises.

attempted.md.primary: Having been tried or undertaken, often unsuccessfully or without full fruition.
attempted.md.secondary: In legal indictments, qualifying a substantive criminal charge where execution fell short of completion.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: You are to know that prosperously I have **attempted**, and with bloody passage led your wars even to the gates of Rome.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: As the crook had absorbed most of Gabriel's money, he **attempted**, and carried out, an exchange of his overcoat for a shepherd's regulation smock-frock.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: It constituted the entire idea among the Hebrews, up to the birth of Christianity, as might be expected in the case of a people whose laws **attempted** to embrace all subjects on which precepts were required.

attempter.md.primary: A person who undertakes an effort, essay, enterprise, or hostile assault.
attempter.md.secondary: In archaic and early modern English, an assailant who assays a fortress or makes an aggressive trial against authority.

quotes.author: John Milton
quotes.quote: The bold **attempter** of the celestial throne surveyed the gulf of darkness stretching beneath him.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: Every daring **attempter** of the imperial purple found eager partisans among the mutinous frontier legions.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: The rash **attempter** who seeks innovation without maturity of counsel meets inevitable disaster.

contemplate.md.primary: To look at or view with continued attention; to observe thoughtfully or meditate deeply upon.
contemplate.md.secondary: In philosophical theology, to engage in intuitive intellectual beholding of transcendent or ultimate truths.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: So many hours must I tend my flock; so many hours must I take my rest; so many hours must I **contemplate**; so many hours must I sport myself.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: It was with gloom he considered on landing at Liverpool that if he were to go home his reception would be of a kind very unpleasant to **contemplate**.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Farebrother, my dear sir, is a man deeply painful to **contemplate**.

contemplation.md.primary: The action of looking thoughtfully at something for a long time; deep reflective thought.
contemplation.md.secondary: In monastic mysticism, a quiet affective communion with the divine beyond reasoned discursive meditation.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: And did you leave him in this **contemplation**?

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: When the waggon had passed on, Gabriel withdrew from his point of espial, and descending into the road, followed the vehicle to the turnpike-gate, where the object of his **contemplation** now halted for the payment of toll.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: Meditation and water are wedded for ever in solemn **contemplation**.

contemplative.md.primary: Expressing, involving, or given to prolonged and serious meditation or reflective thought.
contemplative.md.secondary: In ecclesiastical classification, designating religious orders whose primary vocation is prayer, silence, and enclosure.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: That fools should be so deep-**contemplative**, and I did laugh sans intermission an hour by his dial.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Nevertheless, though the novel was intended to be neither didactic nor aggressive, in the **contemplative** parts it was oftener charged with impressions than with convictions.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Cadwallader's errand could not be despatched in the presence of grooms, so she asked to be taken into the conservatory close by, and on coming to a **contemplative** stand, she spoke.

contemplativeness.md.primary: A persistent habit or disposition of engaging in deep, serious, and tranquil reflection.
contemplativeness.md.secondary: In aesthetic psychology, the meditative repose that permits disinterested observation of beauty or artistic forms.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
quotes.quote: There is a quiet **contemplativeness** in the fisherman's posture that harmonizes with the gentle motion of the stream.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: The solitary recluse preserved a serene **contemplativeness** amidst the noisy bustle of the growing township.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Her face wore that settled **contemplativeness** which comes from long hours spent beside the quiet hearth.

contemporaneity.md.primary: The state or fact of existing, occurring, or flourishing during the same period of time.
contemporaneity.md.secondary: In historical geology and paleontology, the synchronicity of stratigraphic strata across geographically distant formations.

quotes.author: Charles Lyell
quotes.quote: The apparent **contemporaneity** of widely separated fossil deposits must be evaluated with extreme caution by the field geologist.

quotes.author: John Phillips
quotes.quote: Smith traced the lines of **contemporaneity** across the stratified formations of the British Isles with singular accuracy.

quotes.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
quotes.quote: Similarity of organic forms in distant strata does not necessarily prove absolute geological **contemporaneity**.

contemporaneous.md.primary: Existing, occurring, originating, or living in the same historical era or chronological period.
contemporaneous.md.secondary: In evidentiary jurisprudence, statements made simultaneously with an event that fall under the res gestae doctrine.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Until the existence of this **contemporaneous** Wessex was acknowledged, the rustic customs were regarded as entirely obsolete.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: The cold may have come on, or have ceased, earlier at one point of the globe than at another, but several large areas were **contemporaneous** in their glacial phenomena.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The testimonies of **contemporaneous** Greek historians corroborate the swift decline of the Roman military frontier.

contemporaneously.md.primary: In a manner occurring, developing, or coexisting at the very same time or period.
contemporaneously.md.secondary: In historiographical analysis, recording observations parallel to events without retrospective distortion.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: I am not, I trust, mistaken in the recognition of some deeper correspondence than that of date in the events unfolding **contemporaneously** around us.

quotes.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotes.quote: The negotiations were conducted **contemporaneously** in London and Paris with the utmost secrecy.

quotes.author: Herbert Spencer
quotes.quote: Various physical forces act **contemporaneously** upon the evolving organism to shape its structural adaptation.

contemporaneousness.md.primary: The characteristic of existing, developing, or taking place at the identical point in time.
contemporaneousness.md.secondary: In modern literary theory, the perceived immediacy and shared temporal horizon uniting author and audience.

quotes.author: William Hazlitt
quotes.quote: The sheer **contemporaneousness** of popular gossip lends it an ephemeral brilliance that quickly fades with the season.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: A novel achieves vivid realism when it conveys the felt **contemporaneousness** of every human heartbeat in the narrative.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: The **contemporaneousness** of two related phenomena does not of itself establish direct reciprocal causation.

contemporaries.md.primary: Persons living, creating, or flourishing at the same historical period as one another.
contemporaries.md.secondary: In sociology and generational cohorts, peer groups subject to the same transformative socio-political events.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Her straw bonnet, which our **contemporaries** might look at with conjectural curiosity as at an obsolete form of basket, fell a little backward.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: Next to his reserve and the faultless propriety of his conduct, his **contemporaries** at college seemed most impressed by the great maturity of his mind.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: He is not fed, sheltered, clothed, warmed, like his **contemporaries**.

contemporary.md.primary: Belonging to, occurring in, or characteristic of the present time or a shared historical era.
contemporary.md.secondary: In art criticism and architecture, creative practice produced after the mid-twentieth century breaking with historicist forms.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Old Mr Clare was a clergyman of a type which, within the last twenty years, has well nigh dropped out of **contemporary** life.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The hall furniture comprised a piece of carving by a **contemporary** of Gibbons.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: This pile of chivalry, which seems so fair to those who look at the **contemporary** facts for science or entertainment, is not equally pleasant to all spectators.

contemporise.md.primary: To cause things to synchronize in time, or to adapt something historical to current sensibilities.
contemporise.md.secondary: In dramaturgy and stage production, setting an ancient or classical drama within a present-day cultural milieu.

quotes.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotes.quote: The director resolved to **contemporise** the Elizabethan dialogue so that modern audiences might grasp its satirical sting.

quotes.author: Walter Pater
quotes.quote: The humanist essayists sought to **contemporise** classical virtues for the emerging civic society of their day.

quotes.author: Oscar Wilde
quotes.quote: To **contemporise** every ancient myth with crude realism is to strip romantic art of its imaginative veil.

contemporize.md.primary: To place, coordinate, or represent occurrences within the same contemporary timeframe.
contemporize.md.secondary: In chronometry and computational historiography, aligning divergent epochal calendars onto a single synchronized timeline.

quotes.author: Henry Adams
quotes.quote: The historian must strive to **contemporize** contradictory archival narratives before attempting a coherent synthesis.

quotes.author: Matthew Arnold
quotes.quote: We must **contemporize** our intellectual ideals with the practical demands of modern industrial democracy.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: The antiquarian endeavors to **contemporize** the remote feudal struggles with our own political factions.

contempt.md.primary: The feeling that a person or a thing is beneath consideration, worthless, or deserving scorn.
contempt.md.secondary: In procedural jurisprudence, willful disobedience to or open disrespect for the lawful authority of a court or legislature.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Why, what place make you special, when you put off that with such **contempt**?

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: In those earlier days she had always nourished a secret **contempt** for girls who were the slaves of the first good-looking young fellow.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: No one of those who profess the most sublime **contempt** for the consequences of actions as an element in their morality attaches more importance to the distinction than I do.

contemptibility.md.primary: Utter unworthiness, baseness, or despicable character deserving universal scorn.
contemptibility.md.secondary: In ethical philosophy, the status of an agent who has thoroughly repudiated honor, duty, and civic obligation.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: Nothing sinks a claimant so swiftly into utter **contemptibility** as the boast of virtues which his conduct belies.

quotes.author: Edmund Burke
quotes.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
quotes.quote: The frivolous antics of the Parisian demagogues exposed their political program to universal **contemptibility**.

quotes.author: Jonathan Swift
quotes.quote: The meager pretensions of the Grub Street scribblers revealed the naked **contemptibility** of their learning.

contemptible.md.primary: Deserving of contempt, scorn, or extreme disdain; despicable and low in estimation.
contemptible.md.secondary: In moral satire, characterizing individuals whose cowardly venality invites public ridicule and reprobation.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Heaven and our Lady gracious hath it pleased to shine on my **contemptible** estate.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Bathsheba demurely regarded a **contemptible** straw lying upon the ground, in a way which suggested less ovine criticism than womanly embarrassment.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Might, could, would—they are **contemptible** auxiliaries.

contemptibly.md.primary: In a manner that excites or thoroughly deserves scorn, disdain, or mean reprobation.
contemptibly.md.secondary: In behavioral critique, acting with such petty malice or cowardice as to degrade personal dignity.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: He isolated himself till the space he filled in the public eye was **contemptibly** small.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: Sometimes he was **contemptibly** childish.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: In common life we esteem but meanly and **contemptibly** a fellow who anoints his hair, and palpably smells of that anointing.

contemptuous.md.primary: Showing, feeling, or expressing deep hatred, scorn, or arrogant disrespect toward others.
contemptuous.md.secondary: In interpersonal communication, facial micro-expressions such as unilateral lip curl that signal perceived superiority.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: **Contemptuous** base-born callet as she is, she vaunted 'mongst her minions t'other day the very train of her worst wearing gown was better worth than all my father's lands.

quotes.author: Lewis Carroll
quotes.quote: When the sands are all dry, he is gay as a lark, and will talk in **contemptuous** tones of the Shark.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Featherstone handed back the letter to him with a **contemptuous** gesture, saying you don't suppose I believe a thing because Bulstrode writes it out fine.

contemptuously.md.primary: In a scornful, haughty, or derisive manner that clearly exhibits complete disdain.
contemptuously.md.secondary: In judicial proceedings, dismissing an opponent's specious arguments with manifest judicial disregard.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: As in revenge of thy ingratitude, I throw thy name against the bruising stones, trampling **contemptuously** on thy disdain.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: What, did you think I should break in? said Boldwood, **contemptuously**.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: They **contemptuously** ask, what right hast thou to be happy? A question which Carlyle pressed with unsparing force.

contemptuousness.md.primary: A persistent disposition or habit of looking down upon others with haughty arrogance.
contemptuousness.md.secondary: In character study and dramatic dialogue, the cold superciliousness of an aristocrat scorning popular sentiment.

quotes.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotes.quote: There was a frosty **contemptuousness** in Blanche Ingram's gaze that withered every humble domestic dependent.

quotes.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotes.quote: The Marquis treated the entreaties of his creditors with habitual aristocratic **contemptuousness**.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Osmond's quiet **contemptuousness** toward American provincialism was masked beneath impeccably polished manners.

distemper.md.primary: A disordered physical or mental state; a contagious viral disease affecting domestic animals.
distemper.md.secondary: In historical painting and interior decor, a water-based paint using animal glue or casein as an adhesive binder.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: If you are sick at sea or stomach-qualmed at land, a dram of this will drive away **distemper**.

quotes.author: Mary Shelley
quotes.quote: She attended her sickbed; her watchful attentions triumphed over the malignity of the **distemper**.

quotes.author: John Milton
quotes.quote: Thus Eve with countenance blithe her story told; but in her cheek **distemper** flushing glowed.

extemporaneous.md.primary: Spoken, performed, composed, or executed on the spur of the moment without prior preparation.
extemporaneous.md.secondary: In competitive forensics and public debate, delivery where arguments are outlined in advance but delivered without a script.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: Your own gift you can present every moment with the cumulative force of a whole life's cultivation; but of the adopted talent of another, you have only an **extemporaneous**, half possession.

quotes.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotes.quote: His **extemporaneous** eloquence in the House of Commons swayed votes that weeks of private lobbying could not shake.

quotes.author: Mark Twain
quotes.quote: It usually takes me more than three weeks to prepare a good **extemporaneous** speech that sounds genuinely spontaneous.

extemporaneously.md.primary: Without premeditation, rehearsals, or prepared notes; in a spontaneous improvised manner.
extemporaneously.md.secondary: In homiletics and parliamentary rhetoric, preaching or arguing fluently from general knowledge without written text.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: Mr. Snodgrass recited several romantic stanzas **extemporaneously** to the astonishment of the assembled rural club.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: The venerable minister addressed the flock **extemporaneously**, his solemn words flowing directly from inward inspiration.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: Holmes deduced the traveler's past career **extemporaneously**, glancing merely at the mud stains upon his boots.

extemporarily.md.primary: In an impromptu or extemporary manner; without previous study, premeditation, or design.
extemporarily.md.secondary: In theatrical improvisation, improvising comic stage business and dialogue to accommodate unexpected audience reactions.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: The quick comedians **extemporarily** will stage us, and present our Alexandrian revels.

quotes.author: Ben Jonson
quotes.quote: He will compose a sonnet **extemporarily** upon any subject you please, before the candle burns down an inch.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: Many young speakers vanity prompts to deliver their judgments **extemporarily**, risking foolish blunders for brief applause.

extemporary.md.primary: Made, done, or uttered on the spur of the occasion; impromptu and lacking formal premeditation.
extemporary.md.secondary: In ecclesiastical history, spontaneous spoken prayers contrasted with prescribed liturgical texts from a prayer book.

quotes.author: Thomas Fuller
quotes.quote: His devotion shone brightest in **extemporary** prayer, when fervent piety supplied the absence of written liturgy.

quotes.author: Joseph Addison
quotes.quote: An **extemporary** assembly gathered quickly in the coffeehouse upon hearing the startling continental rumors.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: He condemned the practice of burdening youth with **extemporary** tasks before fundamental principles were thoroughly grounded.

extempore.md.primary: Carried out, spoken, or composed without preparation; impromptu or on the spur of the moment.
extempore.md.secondary: In classical musical performance, improvising a cadenza or accompaniment over a figured bass line.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: O villain, thou stolest a cup of sack eighteen years ago, and wert taken with the manner, and ever since thou hast blushed **extempore**.

quotes.author: Samuel Pepys
quotes.quote: The parson preached an **extempore** sermon of an hour long, which pleased the congregation exceedingly well.

quotes.author: Jonathan Swift
quotes.quote: The enthusiastic preacher poured forth his **extempore** meditations with uncommon zeal and vehement gestures.

extemporisation.md.primary: The act of performing, composing, or improvising speech or music without previous preparation.
extemporisation.md.secondary: In musical history and theater, extemporisation formed a core improvisational skill in commedia dell'arte and baroque ornamentation.

quotes.author: Charles Burney
quotes.quote: The Italian organist displayed astonishing mastery in his brilliant **extemporisation** upon the fugue subject.

quotes.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
quotes.quote: True poetic brilliance relies rarely on hasty **extemporisation**, but rather upon long-cherished imaginative meditation.

quotes.author: William Hazlitt
quotes.work: Lectures on the English Comic Writers
quotes.quote: His rapid comedic **extemporisation** carried the audience forward in waves of irresistible laughter.

extemporise.md.primary: To compose, perform, or deliver something spontaneously without notes or prior rehearsal.
extemporise.md.secondary: In jazz harmony and soloing, to extemporise melodic variations across complex chord progressions.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: The country fiddler began to **extemporise** lively dance variations that set every rustic foot tapping.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: She sat at the piano, beginning to **extemporise** plaintive chords that mirrored the sorrow of her soul.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: Sherlock Holmes took up his violin to **extemporise** strange, mournful melodies through the foggy evening.

extemporization.md.primary: An impromptu speech, composition, or musical piece executed without advance planning.
extemporization.md.secondary: In classical oratory and forensics, extemporization allows a debater to counter hostile cross-examination with agile counterarguments.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The eloquent **extemporization** of the Christian bishop astonished the pagan magistrates assembled in the basilica.

quotes.author: Thomas De Quincey
quotes.quote: His wondrous **extemporization** of musical fantasies transported the listener into boundless dreamscapes.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Her impassioned **extemporization** from the speaker's platform held the assembly in breathless suspense.

extemporize.md.primary: To speak, perform, or fashion something extemporaneously using whatever materials are at hand.
extemporize.md.secondary: In expeditionary survival and field medicine, to extemporize emergency splints or shelters from wilderness debris.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: The shepherd had to **extemporize** a shelter from hurdles and straw against the sudden pelting rain.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The carpenter could **extemporize** any needed tool or prosthetic limb from spare whalebone and seasoned pine.

quotes.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotes.quote: We were forced to **extemporize** a barricade across the blockhouse door using heavy pork casks and timber.

intemperance.md.primary: Lack of moderation, balance, or self-restraint; excessive indulgence in appetites or passions.
intemperance.md.secondary: In the nineteenth-century temperance movement, habitual abuse of ardent spirits regarded as the root of moral decay.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: This in the name of God I promise here, that I shall perform, and beseech your Majesty may salve the long-grown wounds of my **intemperance**.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Raffles proved more unmanageable, his chronic state of mental restlessness, the growing effect of habitual **intemperance**, quickly shaking off every impression.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: We have found out fine names to cover our sensuality withal, but no gifts can raise **intemperance**.

intemperate.md.primary: Showing a lack of self-control; given to excessive consumption, fiery passions, or severe weather.
intemperate.md.secondary: In climatology and historical geography, an intemperate climate characterized by violent extremes of heat or cold.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: He would not, but by gift of my chaste body to his concupiscible **intemperate** lust, release my brother.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: Who is that **intemperate** and brutal man whom we would redeem?

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: **Intemperate** habits are so highly destructive, that the expectation of life of the intemperate, at the age of thirty, is only thirteen years.

intemperately.md.primary: In an immoderate, unrestrained, or excessively passionate manner lacking all moderation.
intemperately.md.secondary: In parliamentary polemics and judicial review, speaking intemperately by casting vitriolic personal aspersions on opponents.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: He drank **intemperately** of the fiery rum, shouting wild oaths into the howling gale.

quotes.author: Edmund Burke
quotes.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
quotes.quote: The people who behaved very unwisely and **intemperately** on that occasion precipitated the collapse of constitutional order.

quotes.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotes.quote: The zealots argued **intemperately** for severe penal measures against nonconforming clergy.

intemperateness.md.primary: Habitual excess, lack of moderate self-control, or extreme inclemency of weather.
intemperateness.md.secondary: In classical moral philosophy, the soul's surrender of rational governance to uncontrolled appetitive drives.

quotes.author: Robert Boyle
quotes.quote: The sudden **intemperateness** of the air and shifting barometric vapors corrupted the chemical solution.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: The **intemperateness** of his youthful desires clouded his perception of moral duty.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: Philosophers often warned that early **intemperateness** in youth purchases misery for mature years.

temp.md.primary: A temporary worker, especially an office employee hired to fill a short-term clerical vacancy.
temp.md.secondary: In labor economics and modern corporate staffing, temporary administrative employment sourced via third-party agencies.

quotes.author: David Foster Wallace
quotes.quote: The corporate agency dispatched a nervous **temp** to handle word processing and administrative filing.

quotes.author: Douglas Coupland
quotes.work: Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture
quotes.quote: Working as an office **temp** offered just enough money to survive without committing to corporate permanence.

quotes.author: Don DeLillo
quotes.quote: She spent the autumn months as a **temp** in a skyscraper accounting firm, filing receipts under humming fluorescent lights.

temper.md.primary: A person's state of mind seen in terms of their being angry, calm, or unreasonable; or to moderate something.
temper.md.secondary: In metallurgy, to treat steel or glass by heating and cooling to achieve desired hardness and elasticity.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: His captain's heart reneges all **temper** and is become the bellows and the fan to cool a gypsy's lust.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: George was walking on behind me with a **temper** as mild as milk.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: There is no ethical creed which does not **temper** the rigidity of its laws by giving a certain latitude for accommodation to circumstances.

tempera.md.primary: A method of painting with pigments dispersed in an emulsion miscible with water, typically egg yolk.
tempera.md.secondary: In fine art conservation, Italian egg tempera on gessoed poplar panels was the primary medium prior to oil glazing.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.quote: The luminous brilliance of early Florentine **tempera** paintings derives from the purity of their egg yolk emulsion.

quotes.author: Walter Pater
quotes.quote: Botticelli applied fine hatching in **tempera** to render the translucent draperies of his celestial figures.

quotes.author: Giorgio Vasari
quotes.work: Lives of the Most Eminent Painters
quotes.quote: Before the Flemish masters perfected oil painting, every Tuscan workshop labored in traditional egg **tempera**.

temperament.md.primary: A person's or animal's nature, especially as it permanently affects their behavior and mood.
temperament.md.secondary: In keyboard tuning and musical acoustics, equal temperament divides the octave into twelve logarithmically equal semitones.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Such high contentment with such a slight initial performance was a part of the Durbeyfield **temperament**.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: They have usually a fine **temperament** and much tolerance towards the smaller errors of men.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: To admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted **temperament** was to introduce a distracting factor into his mental results.

temperamental.md.primary: Liable to unreasonable changes of mood; erratic, unpredictable, or highly sensitive in behavior.
temperamental.md.secondary: In engineering and mechanics, describing finely tuned machinery prone to erratic malfunctions under slight variations.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: His **temperamental** sensitivity caused him to magnify every imagined slight into a grave dishonor.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.quote: She understood the **temperamental** storms of artistic souls who swung between ecstasy and despair.

quotes.author: E. M. Forster
quotes.quote: The young pianist was notoriously **temperamental**, refusing to play if the drawing room was excessively warm.

temperamentally.md.primary: With regard to natural disposition, emotional tendencies, or constitutional character.
temperamentally.md.secondary: In psychological profiling, innate neurochemical traits governing reactivity and baseline emotional responsiveness.

quotes.author: G. K. Chesterton
quotes.quote: He was **temperamentally** incapable of suspecting his neighbors of calculated villainy.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Strether was **temperamentally** inclined to view European manners with generous indulgence.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Marianne was **temperamentally** disposed to indulge her grief with romantic extravagance.

temperance.md.primary: Abstinence from alcoholic drink; or moderation and voluntary self-restraint in action and thought.
temperance.md.secondary: In classical cardinal virtue ethics, sophrosyne or temperance regulates bodily passions under the direction of reason.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: For I am sure, though you can guess what **temperance** should be, you know not what it is.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: **Temperance** Miller—oh, here's another, Soberness—both women I suppose?

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: The **temperance** of the hero proceeds from the same wish to do no dishonor to the worthiness he has.

temperate.md.primary: Showing moderation or self-restraint; or having a mild climate without extremes of temperature.
temperate.md.secondary: In physical geography, the temperate zones lying between the tropics and the polar circles characterized by four distinct seasons.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Whiles yet the cool and **temperate** wind of grace o'erblows the filthy and contagious clouds of heady murder, spoil, and villainy.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Full of this dim and **temperate** bliss, he went on to fling the ewe over upon her other side.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: Species from an arctic or even from a **temperate** region cannot endure a tropical climate, or conversely.

temperately.md.primary: In a moderate, calm, and restrained manner; without violence, excess, or passion.
temperately.md.secondary: In ethical deliberation, addressing contentious disputes with measured civility and dispassionate logic.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Corinthian, speak **temperately**, and let thy words answer with wisdom.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: He who lives **temperately** and drinks only spring water finds life sweetened with simple pleasures.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: The sage expounded his doctrines **temperately**, avoiding dogmatic vehemence while imparting wisdom.

temperateness.md.primary: The quality of moderation, mildness of climate, or freedom from excessive passions.
temperateness.md.secondary: In environmental geography, the favorable atmospheric equability of regions shielded from continental thermal extremes.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: The **temperateness** of his disposition preserved his judgment intact during times of political faction.

quotes.author: Edmund Burke
quotes.quote: The **temperateness** of the autumn breeze produces an agreeable languor throughout the senses.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: Habitual **temperateness** in diet and exercise is the surest foundation of physical longevity.

temperature.md.primary: The degree or intensity of heat present in a substance or object, expressed on a comparative scale.
temperature.md.secondary: In thermodynamics, a macroscopic measure of the average kinetic energy of constituent particles within a system.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Farmer Oak considered that he would first sit down leaving both closed, till the **temperature** of the hut was a little raised.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: Differences in nests depend on the situations chosen, and on the nature and **temperature** of the country inhabited.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Much sustained by application of the thermometer which implied the importance of his **temperature**, he endured his illness.

tempered.md.primary: Having been adjusted, hardened, or moderated by blending, heat treatment, or experience.
tempered.md.secondary: In metallurgy, steel subjected to controlled reheating after quenching to increase toughness while reducing brittleness.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: So wouldst thou, if the truth of thy love to me were so righteously **tempered** as mine is to thee.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Oak belonged to the even-**tempered** order of humanity, and felt the secret fusion of himself in Bathsheba to be burning with a finer flame.

quotes.author: Lewis Carroll
quotes.quote: Maybe it's always pepper that makes people hot-**tempered**, she went on, very much pleased at having found out a new kind of rule.

tempering.md.primary: The process of moderating, softening, or toughening a material or human attitude.
tempering.md.secondary: In chocolate manufacturing, controlled crystallization of cocoa butter polymorphs to ensure a glossy sheen and crisp snap.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: I have him already **tempering** between my finger and my thumb, and shortly will I seal with him.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Brooke spoke of meeting people half-way, **tempering** your ideas, and saying well now there's something in that.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: As the blacksmith was about giving the barbs their final heat, prior to **tempering** them, he cried to Ahab to place the water-cask near.

tempest.md.primary: A violent, windy storm accompanied by rain, hail, or snow; or an emotional tumult.
tempest.md.secondary: In meteorological history, severe maritime squalls capable of foundering sailing vessels and altering coastlines.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: In the very torrent, **tempest**, and whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that may give it smoothness.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Like a steady ship doth strongly part the raging waves and keeps her course aright; ne aught for **tempest** doth from it depart.

quotes.author: Oscar Wilde
quotes.quote: She was a curious woman, whose dresses always looked as if they had been designed in a rage and put on in a **tempest**.

tempest-swept.md.primary: Buffeted, battered, or repeatedly scourged by violent gales and oceanic storms.
tempest-swept.md.secondary: In littoral ecology, harsh coastal headlands where vegetation is stunted and flag-formed by persistent marine squalls.

quotes.author: Alfred Tennyson
quotes.quote: Upon the **tempest-swept** cliffs of Cornwall, the lonely fortress stood against the foam.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The **tempest-swept** decks of the Pequod ran white with frothing brine during the midnight squall.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Across the **tempest-swept** expanse of Egdon Heath, the ancient barrows loomed like sleeping titans.

tempest-tossed.md.primary: Violently driven, buffeted, or agitated by furious ocean gales or emotional strife.
tempest-tossed.md.secondary: In maritime literature and immigration allegories, ships navigating mountainous seas before reaching safe harbor.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Though his bark cannot be lost, yet it shall be **tempest-tossed**.

quotes.author: Walt Whitman
quotes.quote: O Captain! my Captain! our fearful trip is done, the **tempest-tossed** ship has weather'd every rack.

quotes.author: Emma Lazarus
quotes.quote: Send these, the homeless, **tempest-tossed** to me, I lift my lamp beside the golden door.

tempest-tost.md.primary: Buffeted and tossed about violently by storms; an archaic variant of tempest-tossed.
tempest-tost.md.secondary: In early modern English poetry and maritime ballads, describing vessels battered by tempestuous ocean waves.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Though his bark cannot be lost, yet it shall be **tempest-tost**.

quotes.author: John Milton
quotes.quote: As when a **tempest-tost** vessel enters the sheltered roadstead after long weeks on the main.

quotes.author: Alexander Pope
quotes.quote: The **tempest-tost** wanderer reached the Phaeacian shores, spent with swimming against the surge.

tempestuous.md.primary: Characterized by strong and turbulent or conflicting emotion; or stormy, turbulent weather.
tempestuous.md.secondary: In atmospheric dynamics, cyclonic disturbances generating severe gale-force winds and torrential squalls.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Like as rigor of **tempestuous** gusts provokes the mightiest hulk against the tide, so am I driven by breath of her renown.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: I remembered his abject pleading, his abject threats, and the **tempestuous** anguish of his soul.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: It stood on a sharp bleak corner, where that **tempestuous** wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than ever it did about poor Paul's tossed craft.

tempestuousness.md.primary: Violent storminess, severe turbulence of weather, or extreme emotional agitation.
tempestuousness.md.secondary: In romantic literary criticism, the sublime fury and emotional violence characteristic of Byronic protagonists.

quotes.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotes.quote: The wild **tempestuousness** of the October night rattled the casements of Thornfield Hall.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: She shuddered at the dark **tempestuousness** of his sudden rage, which shattered their peaceful reverie.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: The gathering **tempestuousness** of the Parisian mob swept away the fragile barriers of the royal guard.

templar.md.primary: A member of the Knights Templar, a medieval devout military religious order founded in 1119.
templar.md.secondary: In English legal history, a barrister or student residing at the Inner Temple or Middle Temple Inns of Court.

quotes.author: Walter Scott
quotes.quote: The fierce **Templar** Brian de Bois-Guilbert rode proudly into the lists, his white mantle bearing the red cross.

quotes.author: Charles Lamb
quotes.quote: I was born, and passed the first seven years of my life, in the Temple: its cheerful **Templar** gardens are dear to memory.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: The veteran knight recalled encounters with the haughty **Templar** commanders in the Syrian borderlands.

template.md.primary: A shaped piece of metal, wood, or plastic used as a pattern for cutting, shaping, or drilling.
template.md.secondary: In molecular biology and genetics, a single strand of DNA that directs the synthesis of a complementary messenger RNA strand.

quotes.author: Francis Crick
quotes.quote: Each strand of the unwound double helix acts as a direct molecular **template** for replicating the complementary chain.

quotes.author: David Starr Jordan
quotes.quote: The master builder constructs his arch over a rigid wooden **template** to ensure flawless curvature.

quotes.author: Thomas Huxley
quotes.quote: The artisan traces his pattern upon the stone slab using an iron **template** to preserve uniform proportions.

temple.md.primary: A building devoted to the worship of a god or gods; or the flat anatomical region on each side of the forehead.
temple.md.secondary: In cranial osteology, the temporal fossa located superior to the zygomatic arch and anterior to the ear.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: A man may, if he were of a fearful heart, stagger in this attempt, for here we have no **temple** but the wood, no assembly but horn-beasts.

quotes.author: Jonathan Swift
quotes.quote: Over against this **temple**, on the other side of the great highway, at twenty feet distance, there was a turret at least five feet high.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: He leaves all his deliverance to God, contenting himself with this, that spite of all his pains and pangs, he will still look towards His holy **temple**.

templet.md.primary: A pattern, mold, or gauge used as a guide in woodworking, metalworking, masonry, or shipbuilding.
templet.md.secondary: In structural masonry and civil engineering, a bearing stone or timber embedded in a wall to distribute concentrated girder loads.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.quote: The Gothic stonecutter dressed the intricate profile of the capital using an accurate zinc **templet**.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: The master builder fits each ashlar block exactly to the prescribed iron **templet**.

quotes.author: William Morris
quotes.quote: The craftsman rejects the dead uniformity of the mechanical **templet** in favor of living handiwork.

templetonia.md.primary: A genus of Australian flowering shrubs in the legume family Fabaceae, including the desert coral bush.
templetonia.md.secondary: In systematic botany, Templetonia retusa produces vivid red papilionaceous flowers adapted for ornithophilous bird pollination.

quotes.author: Ferdinand von Mueller
quotes.quote: On dry limestone ridges, the showy **Templetonia** displays its crimson blossoms through midwinter.

quotes.author: Joseph Maiden
quotes.work: The Useful Native Plants of Australia
quotes.quote: The red-flowering shrub known as **Templetonia** thrives in coastal dunes, resisting saline sea winds.

quotes.author: Robert Brown
quotes.quote: We classified the newly discovered legume under the genus **Templetonia** in honor of our esteemed colleague.

tempo.md.primary: The speed at which a passage of music is or should be played; or the pace of any ongoing activity.
tempo.md.secondary: In chess strategy and tactical endgame theory, a turn to move seen as a valuable unit of initiative.

quotes.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotes.quote: The conductor took the allegro at such a breathless **tempo** that the woodwinds were hopelessly scrambled.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.quote: The rapid **tempo** of the London traffic set the pulse of modern life racing through the streets.

quotes.author: E. M. Forster
quotes.quote: She adjusted herself to the quiet, pastoral **tempo** of Hertfordshire farm life after the roar of town.

temporal.md.primary: Relating to worldly as opposed to spiritual affairs; or of or relating to time as measured sequentially.
temporal.md.secondary: In cranial anatomy, pertaining to the temporal bone, temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex, or temples of the skull.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: So children **temporal** fathers do appease; gods are more full of mercy.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: He was anxious to acquire a knowledge of his wife's **temporal** affairs before deciding which to do.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: Never raising any superstructure until we found a better reason for it than our **temporal** necessities even.

temporalis.md.primary: A broad, fan-shaped muscle on each side of the head that elevates and retracts the mandible to close the jaw.
temporalis.md.secondary: In human osteology and dental biomechanics, the temporalis muscle originates from the temporal fossa and inserts into the coronoid process.

quotes.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
quotes.work: A Manual of the Anatomy of Vertebrated Animals
quotes.quote: The powerful **temporalis** muscle passes beneath the zygomatic arch to attach firmly upon the coronoid process.

quotes.author: Richard Owen
quotes.quote: In carnivorous mammals, the deep sagittal crest provides extensive surface area for the origin of the massive **temporalis**.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: The reduction in size of the human **temporalis** corresponds with our diminished canine dentition and softened diet.

temporality.md.primary: The state of existing within or having some relationship with time; or a church's worldly property and secular revenues.
temporality.md.secondary: In phenomenological ontology, temporality constitutes the subjective experience and internal flow of past, present, and projected future.

quotes.author: Thomas Aquinas
quotes.quote: Eternal existence transcends the fleeting bounds of mortal **temporality** and worldly succession.

quotes.author: Thomas More
quotes.quote: The disputes between the spiritual hierarchy and the secular **temporality** provoked serious civil discord.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: Man's earthly existence is bound to fragile **temporality**, while divine wisdom endures uncorrupted.

temporally.md.primary: With respect to time; in a temporal sequence; or in a secular, worldly manner as opposed to spiritual.
temporally.md.secondary: In relativistic physics and epistemology, events occurring temporally proximal to each other in a shared frame of reference.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: Memories that are **temporally** contiguous tend to evoke one another through associative neural pathways.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: Ideas presented **temporally** in succession give rise to our fundamental conception of duration.

quotes.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
quotes.quote: The two evolutionary developments did not occur **temporally** side by side, but followed successive geological eras.

temporalty.md.primary: The secular laity as distinguished from the clergy; or secular possessions and revenues of an ecclesiastic.
temporalty.md.secondary: In English constitutional and parliamentary history, the Lords Temporal as distinguished from the Lords Spiritual in Parliament.

quotes.author: William Blackstone
quotes.work: Commentaries on the Laws of England
quotes.quote: The parliament consisted of the lords spiritual, the **temporalty**, and the commons of the realm.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The revenues of the church aroused the jealousy of the feudal **temporalty** throughout medieval Christendom.

quotes.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotes.quote: The bishops clashed frequently with the proud **temporalty** over the assessment of clerical taxes.

temporarily.md.primary: For a limited period of time only; not permanently or enduringly.
temporarily.md.secondary: In contract law, provisional relief or interlocutory injunctions granted temporarily pending full adjudication.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: She had dreaded him, winced before him, then, **temporarily** blinded by his ardent manners, had been stirred to confused surrender awhile.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: No one supposes that the fertility of these animals or plants has been suddenly and **temporarily** increased in any sensible degree.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Fred had a hundred and thirty-five pounds towards meeting the bill, so that the deficit **temporarily** thrown on Mr. Garth was small.

temporariness.md.primary: The property, state, or duration of lasting for only a short or limited time.
temporariness.md.secondary: In existential philosophy and urban sociology, the lived sense of provisional fragility in transient modern dwellings.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: The obvious **temporariness** of the shanty reminded the traveler that human life on earth is merely a bivouac.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: The mind perceives the necessary **temporariness** of all material institutions compared to eternal spiritual truths.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: All social garments and customs wear an stamp of inevitable **temporariness**, changing with each passing epoch.

temporary.md.primary: Lasting for only a limited period of time; not permanent, enduring, or perpetual.
temporary.md.secondary: In civil engineering, temporary works such as falsework, formwork, and shoring used during construction phases.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: I know him for a man divine and holy, not scurvy, nor a **temporary** meddler, as he's reported by this gentleman.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Her wayward sentiment that evening concerning Fanny's **temporary** resting-place had been the result of a strange complication of impulses in Bathsheba's bosom.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: When it means anything better than this, it means that which is expedient for some immediate object, some **temporary** purpose.

temporise.md.primary: To act evasively in order to gain time, defer a decision, or humor the current of circumstances.
temporise.md.secondary: In diplomatic negotiation, adopting calculated procrastination to await shifting geopolitical alliances.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The Roman envoy chose to **temporise** with the barbarian chieftain until the legionary reinforcements arrived from Illyricum.

quotes.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotes.quote: The cautious ministers thought it safer to **temporise** than to provoke an open conflict with the proud barons.

quotes.author: Walter Scott
quotes.quote: He deemed it prudent to **temporise** until he could ascertain which royal claimant held the upper hand.

temporiser.md.primary: A person who temporizes; someone who procrastinates or adapts their conduct to the times.
temporiser.md.secondary: In political polemics, a trimmer who shifts allegiance opportunistically to remain in government favor.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: The shrewd **temporiser** watches the shifting political winds, ready to cheer whichever faction ascends to power.

quotes.author: Edmund Burke
quotes.work: Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
quotes.quote: The unprincipled **temporiser** sacrifices long-term national honor for the ephemeral advantage of the hour.

quotes.author: Jonathan Swift
quotes.quote: He was ever a cautious **temporiser**, balancing nicely between court factions to secure his personal pension.

temporize.md.primary: To avoid making a firm decision or committing oneself in order to gain time; or to trim.
temporize.md.secondary: In crisis diplomacy, temporizing through procedural delay to allow de-escalation of border tensions.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: All's well, and might have been much better if he could have **temporized**.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: In dangerous affairs, it is sometimes wise to **temporize**, provided delay does not embolden the adversary.

quotes.author: Samuel Samuel Daniel
quotes.quote: They might their grievance inwardly complain, but outwardly they needs must **temporize**.

temporizer.md.primary: One who yields to or temporizes with the times; an opportunistic time-server or compromiser.
temporizer.md.secondary: In parliamentary debate, an unprincipled politician who accommodates opposing sides to preserve ministerial office.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: If thou canst not, thou art an arrogant **temporizer**, and hast no true knowledge of honor.

quotes.author: Walt Whitman
quotes.quote: Not a word for the corrupt **temporizer** or the cringing apologist for human bondage.

quotes.author: Robert Burton
quotes.quote: A sort of **temporizers**, ready to embrace and maintain all that is proposed in hope of preferment.

tempra.md.primary: A commercial pharmaceutical brand name for acetaminophen (paracetamol) oral suspension for fever relief.
tempra.md.secondary: In pediatric pharmacology and antipyretic therapeutics, an over-the-counter liquid analgesic formulation devoid of aspirin.

quotes.author: Oliver Sacks
quotes.quote: The pediatric nurse administered a measured teaspoon of **Tempra** drops to lower the child's soaring fever.

quotes.author: Richard Gordon
quotes.quote: The medicine cabinet was stocked with reliable analgesics like **Tempra** and simple calamine lotion.

quotes.author: Lewis Thomas
quotes.work: The Youngest Science: Notes of a Medicine-Watcher
quotes.quote: In modern pediatric practice, formulations such as **Tempra** swiftly superseded the traditional sponging baths.

tempt.md.primary: To entice or attempt to entice someone to do something, often something unwise or immoral.
tempt.md.secondary: In classical theology, an enticement that tests moral resolve or provokes divine retribution.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: **Tempt** him not so too far; I wish, forbear.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Put your hand upon that stone hand, and swear that you will never **tempt** me by your charms or ways.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: The mistletoe may metaphorically be said to struggle with other fruit-bearing plants, in order to **tempt** birds to devour and thus disseminate its seeds.

temptable.md.primary: Susceptible to temptation, seduction, or moral inducement; easily influenced to do wrong.
temptable.md.secondary: In psychological forensics and moral theology, possessing a vulnerable disposition prone to ethical compromise under stress.

quotes.author: Ralph Cudworth
quotes.work: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
quotes.quote: Mortal nature is frail and **temptable**, easily seduced from heavenly virtue by the allurements of the senses.

quotes.author: Jeremy Taylor
quotes.quote: A man must remember that his flesh is ever **temptable**, requiring constant vigilance and fasting.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Tito's nature was too fluid and **temptable** to withstand the golden promises of political intrigue.

temptation.md.primary: The desire to do something, especially something wrong or unwise; or an attractive thing enticing one to act.
temptation.md.secondary: In ascetical theology, spiritual trials permitted by providence to purify human fidelity and test moral perseverance.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Those pretty wrongs that liberty commits, when I am sometime absent from thy heart, thy beauty, and thy years full well befits, for still **temptation** follows where thou art.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Bathsheba paused, as if about to refuse a reply, but the **temptation** to say yes was irresistible.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: It may be objected, that many who are capable of the higher pleasures, occasionally, under the influence of **temptation**, postpone them to the lower.

tempter.md.primary: A person or entity that entices or prompts someone to commit a wrongful, sinful, or foolish act.
tempter.md.secondary: In Christian demonology and scripture, an appellation for Satan as the supreme instigator of human transgression.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: The **tempter** or the tempted, who sins most, ha?

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: Over and over again, the **tempter** of souls had thrust this idea upon Hester's contemplation.

quotes.author: John Milton
quotes.quote: So glozed the **Tempter**, and his proem tuned; into the heart of Eve his words made way.

tempting.md.primary: Appealing or attractive, especially in a way that creates an urge to possess, consume, or indulge.
tempting.md.secondary: In consumer psychology and culinary arts, visual presentation crafted to stimulate visceral appetite and purchase desire.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.work: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Ay me, but yet thou mightst my seat forbear, thine by thy beauty **tempting** her to thee, thine by thy beauty being false to me.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: No, we won't toss money on a Sunday, that would be **tempting** the devil indeed.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: All the light I can command must be concentrated on this particular web, and not dispersed over that **tempting** range of relevancies called the universe.

temptingly.md.primary: In an enticing, alluring, or seductive manner that invites indulgence or curiosity.
temptingly.md.secondary: In gastronomic description, arranging delicacies so as to appeal irresistibly to sight and olfactory senses.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The hot roast fowl and buttered rolls were laid out **temptingly** before the weary travelers at the coaching inn.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: The ripe strawberries hung **temptingly** from the vines in the pleasant shade of Donwell Abbey.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: The forged cheque lay **temptingly** on the desk, offering an easy escape to the desperate cashier.

temptingness.md.primary: The seductive power, attractiveness, or charm that entices someone toward desire or indulgence.
temptingness.md.secondary: In moral philosophy and market psychology, the compelling allure exerted by illicit gains or luxury commodities.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: The fatal **temptingness** of sudden riches has ruined many an honest tradesman's integrity.

quotes.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotes.quote: Becky Sharp understood the dangerous **temptingness** of her coquettish glances upon naive young subalterns.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: The subtle **temptingness** of the Venetian palace whispered of boundless romantic possibilities.

temptress.md.primary: A woman who entices or seduces someone, especially toward romantic or moral indiscretion.
temptress.md.secondary: In literary archetypes and dramatic tragedy, the femme fatale who ensnares heroes and precipitates their downfall.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: She felt a bitter pang when the malicious village tongues branded her an immoral **temptress**.

quotes.author: Walter Scott
quotes.quote: She was my **temptress**, the foul provoker who drew me from the path of dutiful service.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: The prisoner denounced the adventuress as a deceitful **temptress** who had lured him into criminal folly.

tempura.md.primary: A Japanese dish of seafood or vegetables dipped in a light batter and swiftly deep-fried in hot oil.
tempura.md.secondary: In culinary history and cultural gastronomy, a cooking technique introduced to Japan by Portuguese missionaries in Nagasaki during the sixteenth century.

quotes.author: Lafcadio Hearn
quotes.quote: The aroma of crisp **tempura** frying in sesame oil drifted through the bustling lantern-lit street market of Osaka.

quotes.author: Isabella Bird
quotes.quote: Our courteous host provided a delicate supper of sea-bream and crisp mountain vegetables cooked as **tempura**.

quotes.author: Basil Hall Chamberlain
quotes.quote: Foreign visitors quickly acquire a fondness for **tempura**, admiring the delicate golden crust of the fried prawns.

untempered.md.primary: Not moderated, softened, or restrained; or metal not brought to the proper hardness and toughness.
untempered.md.secondary: In biblical prophecy and architecture, untempered mortar mixed without proper binding agents that collapses under torrential rain.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: Her wild spirit was like an **untempered** steel blade, dangerous to handle and liable to snap under harsh strain.

quotes.author: King James Bible
quotes.quote: One built up a wall, and lo, others daubed it with **untempered** morter: say unto them that daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The harpooneer wielded an iron spear of raw, **untempered** metal that bent against the whale's tough blubber.

untempting.md.primary: Not attractive or appealing to the senses; failing to arouse desire, interest, or appetite.
untempting.md.secondary: In behavioral economics and marketing, offer terms or conditions so disadvantageous that prospective clients immediately decline.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The cold crust of bread and congealed broth looked thoroughly **untempting** upon the rough wooden deal table.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The bleak prospect of trudging through the slushy lanes presented an **untempting** journey to the old weaver.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: The meager salary attached to the remote curacy was singularly **untempting** to ambitious university graduates.
